partTitle: Part Three: The Spirit and the Church
creedLine: I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Amen.

cards.title: The intrinsic unity of the last statements in the Creed
cards.idea: The Creed’s last articles — Church, communion, forgiveness, resurrection — develop one profession: “I believe in Holy Spirit”: God’s saving power in history, where salvation history and the Trinity interlock.
cards.before: Are the Creed’s last articles just a list tacked on after the Christ section, or one single movement? What holds them together?
cards.after: They are one movement: Church, communion of saints, forgiveness of sins, and resurrection all unfold the single profession “I believe in Holy Spirit.” Each names how the Spirit works in history — through baptism, Eucharist, and the final transformation of the world.
cards.why: Ratzinger recovers a lost unity: salvation history and the Trinity once interlocked, so the Spirit article speaks of “God facing outward” — the risen Lord’s power present in history — not merely a third Person in the Godhead.
cards.quote: nothing more than developments of its basic profession, “I believe in Holy Spirit.”

cloze.pre: In other words, the third section of the Creed refers in the first place, not to the Holy Spirit as the third Person in the Godhead, but to the Holy Spirit as
cloze.post: in the community of those who believe in Christ.

cloze.pre: Both statements are to be understood as
cloze.blank: concretizations of the words about the Holy Spirit
cloze.post: , as descriptions of the way in which this Spirit works in history.

cloze.pre: The concluding words of the Creed, too, the profession of faith in the “resurrection of the body” and “life everlasting”, are to be understood as
cloze.blank: the unfolding of faith in the Holy Spirit
cloze.post: and his transforming power, whose final effect they depict.

cards.recall: In your own words, why do the Creed’s last articles — Church, forgiveness, resurrection — count as developments of one statement about the Holy Spirit rather than four separate beliefs?

cards.title: The holy, catholic Church
cards.idea: The Church is holy through God’s power working in sinful members, not their virtue; catholicity is wholeness — visibly one local and universal church around one Word and one table.
cards.before: If the Church is full of scandal and split into rival bodies each claiming to be right, how can anyone honestly say “I believe in the holy, catholic Church”?
cards.after: “Holy” names God’s sanctifying power at work in spite of human sinfulness — the Church is “the shape taken by grace in this world”; “catholic” names her visible unity: one faith, one bread, open to everyone everywhere.
cards.why: Ratzinger turns the objection into the answer: true holiness is “not separation, but union; not judgment, but redeeming love” — God mixing with the dirt of the world to overcome it, which comforts rather than condemns, since all of us are borne up by Christ.
cards.quote: precisely in her paradoxical combination of holiness and unholiness the Church is in fact the shape taken by grace in this world

cloze.pre: The holiness of the Church consists in that
cloze.post: which God exerts in her in spite of human sinfulness.

cloze.pre: He has drawn sin to himself, made it his lot, and so revealed what true “holiness” is: not separation, but union; not judgment, but
This unity is first and foremost the unity of Word and sacrament: the Church is one through
cloze.blank: the one Word and the one bread

cards.recall: Explain in your own words why Ratzinger thinks the Church’s sinfulness confirms rather than disproves her holiness — and what “catholic” demands of local churches today.

cards.title: The resurrection of the body
cards.idea: Resurrection affirms the whole person and the material world against mere survival of the soul: we live on not by our own power but because God knows and loves us.
cards.before: Is “the resurrection of the body” an embarrassing myth for the modern mind, or does it say something about the material world that “immortality of the soul” cannot?
cards.after: It is the Bible’s total answer: the one, undivided, embodied person lives on — awakened by God’s love, in fellowship with all — and matter itself has a future, shown in the risen Lord. It is neither the soul’s automatic survival nor the return of physical bodies.
cards.why: Ratzinger takes on both sides at once: against Greek dualism he insists it is the whole man, not a separated soul, that rises; against naive materialism he reads Paul — “the resurrection of persons”, not of physical bodies, in a transformed form.
cards.quote: they, they themselves, live on; not by virtue of their own power, but because they are known and loved by God

cloze.pre: First of all, the hope for the resurrection of the dead simply represents the basic form of the biblical hope for immortality; it appears in the New Testament not really as a supplement to a preceding and independent immortality of the soul but as
cloze.blank: the fundamental statement on the fate of man

cloze.pre: Immortality as conceived by the Bible proceeds, not from the intrinsic power of what is in itself indestructible, but
cloze.blank: from being drawn into the dialogue with the Creator
cloze.post: ; that is why it must be called awakening.

cloze.pre: One thing at any rate may be fairly clear: both John (6:63) and Paul (1 Cor 15:50) state with all possible emphasis that the “resurrection of the flesh”, the “resurrection of the body”, is

cards.recall: In your own words, explain the difference between the Greek idea of immortality and the biblical idea of resurrection — and why Ratzinger says the risen body is not a physical body.

cards.title: Belief in the Holy Spirit
cards.idea: The Spirit is the risen Christ’s living presence in history, love stronger than death, who makes faith personal and gathers believers into the Church, transforming the world toward resurrection.
cards.before: Is the Holy Spirit just a pious atmosphere the Church invokes, or someone whose arrival actually changes the shape of faith and the shape of the Church?
cards.after: The Spirit is God’s power in history, through whom the risen Lord stays present; faith in the Spirit and faith in the Church belong together from the start. He makes the gift personal — forgiveness creating fellowship — and ecclesial: one bread, one body.
cards.why: Ratzinger warns that when teaching about the Spirit and teaching about the Church split apart, both suffer: the Church becomes a worldly institution and the Spirit “homeless”. Held together, the Creed’s last articles all follow, and the Spirit turns out to be love that overleaps death.
cards.quote: the Holy Spirit as the power through which the risen Lord remains present in the history of the world

cloze.pre: To summarize all this, we can now say that in our Creed the Church is understood
cloze.blank: in terms of the Holy Spirit
cloze.post: , as the center of the Spirit’s activity in the world.

cloze.pre: With this event, as we have seen, the frontier of bios, in other words, death, was crossed and a new continuum was opened up: the biological has been overtaken by the spirit,
cloze.blank: by love, which is stronger than death

cloze.pre: Thus the “objective” view (from the angle of the gift of God)
cloze.blank: brings the personal element into play of its own accord
cloze.post: : the new being of forgiveness leads us into fellowship with those who live from forgiveness; forgiveness establishes communion; and communion with the Lord in the Eucharist leads necessarily to the communion of the converted, who all eat one and the same bread, to become in it “one body” (1 Cor 10:17) and, indeed, “one single new man” (cf. Eph 2:15).

cards.recall: In your own words, how does the Holy Spirit make faith both personal and ecclesial — and why can the Church not be understood apart from him?

cards.title: What it means to say “I believe” today
cards.idea: To believe is to take a trusting stand on ground I did not make: the Creed’s “I believe” becomes “I believe in you” — believing, trusting, and loving become one.
cards.before: After 250 pages of argument, what is actually left of “I believe” — a list of opinions I defend, or something else entirely?
cards.after: Faith is stand-understand, not know-make: entrusting myself to a meaning I did not make and cannot prove, because it upholds me. The whole Creed culminates in a personal act — “I believe in you” — where believing, trusting, and loving fuse into one.
cards.why: Ratzinger’s final twist: faith is not a deficit of knowledge but the human way of standing in reality. Its core is not “I believe in something” but trust in a You; the whole book, he says, circles one question — “Are you really he?”
cards.quote: its central formula is not “I believe in something”, but “I believe in you.”

cloze.pre: Faith is thereby defined as taking up a position, as
cloze.post: on the ground of the word of God.

cloze.pre: Meaning, that is, the ground on which our existence as a totality can stand and live,
cloze.blank: cannot be made but only received

cloze.post: are one, and all the theses around which belief revolves are only concrete expressions of the all-embracing about-turn, of the assertion “I believe in you”—of the discovery of God in the countenance of the man Jesus of Nazareth.

cards.recall: In your own words, explain why Ratzinger says faith is “standing firm” rather than knowing — and what changes when “I believe” becomes “I believe in you”.
